title: Chutes AI Alternatives: Free and Paid Options (2026)
summary: Chutes AI alternatives offer different pricing models and feature sets for inference. Identify which service matches your budget and API requirements.
body_markdown:
## Using Your New Provider Inside Activepieces Workflows


Only if Chutes was powering automations rather than code does Activepieces matter here. It's a workflow tool, not a Chutes alternative, and it hosts no models, though MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production.


So for those workflows switching is a connection change instead of a rewrite. If you call the API only from your own code, skip this section.


### Where it fits and where it doesn't


Activepieces is an open-source AI automation platform with an MIT-licensed core and 750 integrations, meaning most of your existing tools should already have connectors built in.


You build flows from a trigger and a chain of steps, and some of those steps call an AI provider that you choose.


The model itself runs at the provider. Activepieces sends the prompt and passes the response to the next step.


On the Plus plan, at $20 a month, you bring your own AI keys, so every AI step costs 1 credit and the model charge lands on your provider bill at the rate you just compared.


Without your own keys, the same step costs 2 credits on a fast model, 10 on a smart one and 20 on a frontier model, which is the resale rate that bring-your-own-key on Plus and above avoids.


For this article's argument, that separation is useful. If a flow reaches Chutes through a provider connection, the flow's logic (the schedule, the spreadsheet lookup, the downstream HTTP call) doesn't depend on which provider answers.


When you leave Chutes over reliability, model availability or a plan change, the work is in the connection and the model name, not in the flow.


It doesn't fix the constraint you're choosing by.


Activepieces won't make a slow provider fast, lower a per-token rate, or add privacy guarantees; on a bring-your-own-key plan every AI step is 1 credit whichever provider answers, and the rest still comes from the provider you pick.


Check each custom HTTP step. If your Chutes usage goes through one rather than a built-in provider option, you'll be editing a base URL and a key by hand.


### Pointing a workflow at the new provider


In the screenshot, a four-step recruitment flow runs from a schedule trigger to a Google Sheets step that finds open job offers, then a Text AI step called Extract Keywords, then an HTTP step that runs a search.


The Extract Keywords step is selected, and its panel exposes three fields: Provider, Model and Prompt. That's the whole surface you touch when swapping a provider.


The prompt ("Extract top keywords from the job description") stays as it is, and the steps before and after it never see the change.


The panel in the screenshot is set to OpenAI with GPT-4o, which makes a handy test case, though you should pick a current model for your own flow. To run the one-hour test inside a flow:


1. Duplicate the flow so the working version keeps running on its existing provider.
2. Open the Text AI step and change the Provider field to your candidate.
3. Enter the candidate's API key in the connection, and set the Model field to a model that provider currently offers.
4. Run the flow on a small sample and compare the output with what the old provider returned.
5. Check the downstream step. If it expects a particular output shape, such as a comma-separated keyword list, confirm the new model still returns it.


Expect step 5 to be where it fails, because different models format the same instruction differently. If the output breaks the next step, tighten the prompt before you rule the provider out.
